name: Skin-lightening for pregnancy (tablets)

card.summary: Tablets or pills taken during pregnancy in the hope that the baby will be born with lighter skin, reflecting a wider culture of skin-lightening.
card.note: Pregnant users may face health complications for themselves and their children, per reports on skin-lightening products.

quick.overview:
Some pregnant women take tablets or pills in the hope that their child will be born fairer-skinned. A 2020 Der Spiegel report on Ghana, summarised by Wikipedia, described women taking such tablets and others applying bleaching lotion to babies in the hope of improving their prospects.

The practice sits within a long history of skin-lightening for appearance in many regions, where lighter skin has signalled status. Glutathione, an antioxidant the body makes, is described as the most common agent taken by mouth for lightening, though whether it works was still unclear as of 2019.
quick.how: Reports describe oral tablets taken during pregnancy, sometimes alongside creams, with the goal of influencing the baby's skin tone. Specific products and regimens vary and are not covered here.
quick.risks: Reports on skin-lightening products describe risks including mercury-related kidney and neurological problems, steroid effects and hydroquinone-related conditions, and note that pregnant users may face complications affecting themselves and their children. Regulators in several regions restrict mercury and hydroquinone products.

lead: Skin-lightening tablets taken during pregnancy are used in the hope that a child will be born with lighter skin. A 2020 Der Spiegel report on Ghana, summarised in Wikipedia's article on skin whitening, said some pregnant women take tablets with this aim and some apply bleaching lotion to babies.[1]

The practice sits within a broader history of skin-lightening. Light skin has been associated with wealth and status in many societies, and ingested whiteners are historically documented, including powdered pearls in China and arsenic complexion wafers advertised in 1889.[1] Glutathione is described as the most common oral lightening agent, though whether it works was unclear as of 2019.[1]

Wikipedia notes that pregnant users of skin-lightening products may face complications for themselves and their children.[1] No published trial is known to this wiki that has tested whether tablets taken in pregnancy change a baby's skin colour.

chain: Claimed to lighten the baby's skin
angle.text: The aim is a lighter-skinned baby, reflecting beauty and status ideals about fair skin. Users take tablets in pregnancy hoping to influence the child's complexion.

infobox: EU banned hydroquinone in cosmetics in 2000[1]

paras: Skin-lightening practices date to ancient East Asia, where pale skin signalled a life indoors; in Europe, lead-based ceruse was widely used in the Elizabethan era, and in the United States arsenic wafers were advertised in 1889.[1] Surveys cited by Wikipedia reported lightening product use by 77% of Nigerian women in 2013.[1]

Mercury in lightening products is linked to neurological and kidney problems, hydroquinone to conditions including ochronosis and nephrotoxicity, and long-term potent steroids to skin atrophy and other effects.[1] The EU banned hydroquinone in cosmetics in 2000, South Africa has regulated such products since the 1970s, and the WHO has noted significant mercury in products.[1]
The Philippine government is reported to recommend against intravenous glutathione because of possible side effects.[1]

timeline.event: Arsenic complexion wafers advertised in the US.[1]
Der Spiegel reports pregnant women in Ghana taking tablets for fairer babies.[1]
